tasks.title: A Committee Selection
tasks.context: A club has 7 men and 5 women. A committee of 4 people is selected at random from the 12 members.
statements: The total number of possible committees is 792.
There are fewer ways to form a committee with exactly 2 men and 2 women than a committee with exactly 3 men and 1 woman.
The probability that the committee consists of all men is less than 5%.
The probability that the committee contains at least one woman is greater than 90%.
The probability of selecting exactly 2 men and 2 women equals 14/33.
tactical_explanations:
Statement A — False

$$
Total committees = \binom{12}{4}
$$

$$
= 495
$$

= 495.

The statement is false. (792 is actually \binom{12}{5}, a different selection size — a tempting but incorrect distractor.)

Statement B — False

$$
Compare \binom{7}{2}\cdot \binom{5}{2} = 210 to \binom{7}{3}\cdot \binom{5}{1} = 175
$$

The statement is false. Since 210 is greater than 175, the 2-2 split is more common, not fewer — the statement has the comparison backwards.

Statement C — False

$$
P(all men) = \binom{7}{4}/\binom{12}{4}
$$

$$
= 35/495
$$

= 7.07%, which is not less than 5%.

The statement is false. A student who applied the complementary count or swapped the inequality direction would mark the statement true.

Statement D — True

$$
P(at least 1 woman) = 1 − P(all men)
$$

$$
= 1 - 0.0707
$$

= 92.93%, which is greater than 90%.

The statement is true.

Statement E — True

$$
P(2 men, 2 women) = \binom{7}{2}\cdot \binom{5}{2}/\binom{12}{4} = 210/495 = 14/33
$$

210/495 simplifies exactly to 14/33 (dividing numerator and denominator by 15), matching the probability computed in Step 1.

The statement is true.
tasks.solution_overview: Set up the total and the key sub-counts, with 7 men and 5 women, choosing 4 of the 12 total members.

tasks.title: A Poker Hand
tasks.context: A standard 52-card deck (13 ranks × 4 suits) is shuffled, and 5 cards are dealt at random to form a hand.
statements: The total number of distinct 5-card hands is 2,598,960.
A full house (three of one rank plus two of another) is more likely than four of a kind.
A flush (all five cards the same suit) is more likely than a full house.
The probability of getting two pair is greater than 5%.
The probability of a flush is more than 8 times the probability of four of a kind.
tactical_explanations:
Statement A — True

$$
Total 5-card hands = \binom{52}{5}
$$

$$
= 2,598,960
$$

= 2,598,960.

The statement is true.

Statement B — True

$$
Compare 13·\binom{4}{3}·12·\binom{4}{2} = 3,744 to 13·48 = 624
$$

Full house has 3,744 hands versus 624 for four of a kind, so a full house is indeed more likely — six times as likely.

The statement is true.

Statement C — True

$$
Compare \binom{13}{5}·4 = 5,148 to 13·\binom{4}{3}·12·\binom{4}{2} = 3,744
$$

A flush has 5,148 hands versus 3,744 for a full house, so a flush is more likely, even though both are rare.

The statement is true.

Statement D — False

$$
P(two pair) = \binom{13}{2}\cdot \binom{4}{2}²·11·\binom{4}{1}/\binom{52}{5}
$$

$$
= 123,552/2,598,960
$$

= 4.754%, which is not greater than 5%.

The statement is false. A student who applied the complementary count or swapped the inequality direction would mark the statement true.

Statement E — True

$$
Compare 5,148/624 = 8.25 to 8
$$

The statement is true.
tasks.solution_overview: Count each hand type out of the total \binom{52}{5} = 2,598,960 five-card hands.

tasks.title: Restricted Seating
tasks.context: 7 students (4 boys and 3 girls) are seated at random in a row of 7 chairs.
statements: The total number of possible seating arrangements is 5,040.
The number of arrangements in which all 3 girls sit together (in some order) is 720.
The probability that all 3 girls sit together is exactly 1/7.
The probability that boys and girls alternate along the row (in either starting order) is greater than 5%.
The probability that all 3 girls sit together is more than 5 times the probability of an alternating arrangement.
tactical_explanations:
Statement A — True

$$
Total arrangements = 7!
$$

The statement is true.

Statement B — True

$$
Arrangements with girls together = 5!·3!
$$

Treating the 3 girls as a single block gives 5 units to arrange (5!), and the girls can be ordered 3! ways within the block: 5!·3! = 720.

The statement is true.

Statement C — True

$$
P(girls together) = 5!·3!/7! = 720/5,040 = 1/7
$$

720/5,040 simplifies exactly to 1/7, matching the probability from Step 1.

The statement is true.

Statement D — False

$$
P(alternating) = 4!·3!/7! = 144/5,040 = 1/35
$$

$$
= 144/5,040
$$

= 2.86%, which is not greater than 5%.

The statement is false. A student who applied the complementary count or swapped the inequality direction would mark the statement true.

Statement E — False

$$
Compare (1/7)/(1/35) = 5 to "more than 5"
$$

The statement is false. This is the same trap as "exactly at the boundary is not beyond the boundary."
tasks.solution_overview: Set up the total arrangements, and the block-method count for keeping the 3 girls together.

tasks.title: Quality Control Sampling
tasks.context: A shipment contains 20 items, of which 4 are defective. An inspector randomly selects 5 items, without replacement, for testing.
statements: The total number of possible samples of 5 items is 15,504.
The probability that the sample contains exactly 2 defective items is greater than 20%.
The probability that the sample contains no defective items is less than 30%.
The probability that the sample contains at least one defective item is less than 70%.
Among the possible counts of defective items in the sample (0 through 4), exactly 1 defective item is the single most likely outcome.
tactical_explanations:
Statement A — True

$$
Total samples = \binom{20}{5}
$$

$$
= 15,504
$$

= 15,504.

The statement is true.

Statement B — True

$$
P(exactly 2 defective) = \binom{4}{2}\cdot \binom{16}{3}/\binom{20}{5}
$$

$$
= 3,360/15,504
$$

= 21.67%, which is greater than 20%.

The statement is true.

Statement C — True

$$
P(zero defective) = \binom{16}{5}/\binom{20}{5}
$$

$$
= 4,368/15,504
$$

= 28.17%, which is less than 30%.

The statement is true.

Statement D — False

$$
P(at least 1 defective) = 1 − P(zero defective)
$$

$$
= 1 - 0.2817
$$

= 71.83%, which is not less than 70%.

The statement is false. A student who applied the complementary count or swapped the inequality direction would mark the statement true.

Statement E — True

$$
Compare P(0), P(1), P(2), P(3), P(4) directly
$$

= 28.17%.

Comparing all five possible counts: P(0) ≈ 28.17%, P(1) ≈ 46.96%, P(2) ≈ 21.67%, P(3) ≈ 3.10%, P(4) ≈ 0.10%.

The statement is true.
tasks.solution_overview: Apply the hypergeometric counting method: 20 items total, 4 defective, 16 good, sample size 5.

tasks.title: Rolling the Dice
tasks.context: 5 fair six-sided dice are rolled at once, and the 5 results are recorded in order (each die is distinguishable).
statements: The total number of possible outcomes is 7,776.
The probability that all five dice show different numbers is greater than 20%.
The probability that at least two dice show the same number is less than 80%.
The probability that all five dice show different numbers equals exactly 1/6.
If only 3 dice were rolled instead of 5, the probability of all different values would be lower than with 5 dice.
tactical_explanations:
Statement A — True

$$
Total outcomes = 6⁵
$$

Each of the 5 dice has 6 possible outcomes, independently, giving 6⁵ = 7,776 total outcomes.

The statement is true.

Statement B — False

$$
P(all different) = 6·5·4·3·2/6⁵
$$

$$
= 5/54
$$

= 9.26%, which is not greater than 20%.

The statement is false. A student who applied the complementary count or swapped the inequality direction would mark the statement true.

Statement C — False

$$
P(at least two same) = 1 − P(all different)
$$

$$
= 1 - 5
$$

= 95%, which is not less than 80%.

The statement is false. A student who applied the complementary count or swapped the inequality direction would mark the statement true (95%).

Statement D — False

$$
Compare 5/54 to 1/6
$$

$$
= 5/54
$$

= 0.0926.

The statement is false. These are not equal — a common error is to assume each die independently has a 1/6 chance of "being different," but the constraint compounds across all 5 dice.

Statement E — False

$$
Compare P(all different, 3 dice)
$$

$$
= 120/216
$$

= 55.56%.

The statement is false. A student who applied the complementary count or swapped the inequality direction would mark the statement true (55.56%).
tasks.solution_overview: Count outcomes for 5 distinguishable dice, then the sub-case where all five show different numbers.

tasks.title: Find the Missing Value
tasks.context: In a group of n people, every pair of people shakes hands exactly once. The total number of handshakes is 45.
statements: The unknown value n equals 10.
If the group had 12 people instead, the total number of handshakes would be 66.
The number of ways to choose a committee of 3 people from the n people is 120.
The number of ways to arrange all n people in a single row (n!) is greater than 1,000,000.
If the total number of handshakes had been 55 instead of 45, n would equal 11.
tactical_explanations:
Statement A — True

$$
Solve \binom{n}{2} = 45 for n
$$

Solving Cn2 = 45 gives n(n−1) = 90, and n = 10 satisfies this (10·9 = 90), as found in Step 1.

The statement is true.

Statement B — True

$$
\binom{12}{2} = 12·11/2 = 66
$$

\binom{12}{2} = 12·11/2 = 66, confirming the statement.

The statement is true.

Statement C — True

$$
\binom{10}{3} = 10·9·8/3! = 120
$$

With n = 10, \binom{10}{3} = 10!/(3!·7!) = 120, confirming the statement.

The statement is true.

Statement D — True

$$
10! = 3,628,800
$$

The statement is true.

Statement E — True

$$
Solve \binom{n}{2} = 55 for n
$$

Solving Cn2 = 55 gives n(n−1) = 110, and n = 11 satisfies this (11·10 = 110), confirming the statement.

The statement is true.
tasks.solution_overview: Solve for n using the handshake count, where every pair of n people shakes hands exactly once.

tasks.title: Arranging BALLOON
tasks.context: The 7 letters of the word BALLOON (B, A, L, L, O, O, N) are arranged at random in a row. The two L's are identical to each other, and the two O's are identical to each other.
statements: The total number of distinct arrangements is 2,520.
The probability that the two L's are adjacent to each other is 2/7.
The probability that the two L's AND the two O's are both adjacent (each pair sitting together) is greater than 10%.
The probability that the two L's are adjacent equals the probability that the two O's are adjacent.
If all 7 letters had been different (no repeats at all), the total number of arrangements would be less than 2,520.
tactical_explanations:
Statement A — False

$$
Total arrangements = 7!/(2!·2!)
$$

The statement is false. Dividing by only one of the two repeated pairs (forgetting either the L's or the O's) gives the tempting but incorrect 2,520 — you must divide by 2! for each repeated letter.

Statement B — True

$$
P(L's adjacent) = (6!/2!)/(7!/(2!·2!)) = 360/1,260 = 2/7
$$

$$
= 360/1,260
$$

= 28.571%.

Gluing the two L's into one block leaves 6 units to arrange, with the two O's still identical among them, giving 6!/2! = 360 arrangements, so P = 2/7, exactly as stated.

The statement is true.

Statement C — False

$$
P(both pairs adjacent) = 5!/(7!/(2!·2!)) = 120/1,260 = 2/21
$$

$$
= 120/1,260
$$

= 9.52%, which is not greater than 10%.

The statement is false. A student who applied the complementary count or swapped the inequality direction would mark the statement true.

Statement D — True

$$
P(L's adjacent) = P(O's adjacent) = 2/7, by symmetry
$$

$$
= 2/7
$$

= 28.571%.

Both calculations give exactly 360/1,260 by the same symmetric logic — the L's and O's each appear twice, so gluing either pair together leads to an identical count.

The statement is true.

Statement E — False

$$
Compare 7! = 5,040 to 7!/(2!·2!) = 1,260
$$

The statement is false. A student who applied the complementary count or swapped the inequality direction would mark the statement true. The disputed claim is "If all 7 letters had been different (no repeats at all), the total number…."
tasks.solution_overview: Apply the multiset permutation formula, since the two L's are identical and the two O's are identical.

= 13,983,816.

= 0%.

tasks.title: A Round Table
tasks.context: 8 people, including two specific friends A and B, are seated at random around a circular table. Only the relative order of the seats matters - rotating everyone around the table by the same amount counts as the same arrangement, but mirror-image seatings are still counted as different.
statements: The total number of distinct circular arrangements is 5,040.
The probability of event A and B sit next to each other is 2/7.
The probability of event A and B do NOT sit next to each other is less than 70%.
If the same 8 people instead sat in a straight row (not around a table), the probability that A and B are adjacent would be exactly 1/4.
Sitting around a round table makes A and B less likely to end up adjacent than sitting in a straight row would.
tactical_explanations:
Statement A — True

$$
Total circular arrangements = (n−1)! = 7!
$$

The statement is true.

Statement B — True

$$
P(A, B adjacent) = 2·(n−2)!/(n−1)! = 1,440/5,040 = 2/7
$$

1,440/5,040 simplifies exactly to 2/7, matching the probability from Step 1.

The statement is true.

Statement C — False

$$
P(not adjacent) = 1 − 2/7 = 5/7
$$

$$
= 5/7
$$

= 71.43%, which is not less than 70%.

The statement is false. A student who applied the complementary count or swapped the inequality direction would mark the statement true.

Statement D — True

$$
P(A, B adjacent, row) = 2·7!/8! = 1/4
$$

$$
= 10,080/40,320
$$

= 25%.

In a row, gluing A and B into a block gives 2·7! = 10,080 arrangements out of 8! = 40,320 total, so P = 1/4 exactly.

The statement is true.

Statement E — False

$$
Compare 2/7
$$

= 28.57%.

The statement is false. A student who applied the complementary count or swapped the inequality direction would mark the statement true (28.57%).

tasks.title: Chevalier de Méré's Dice Problem
tasks.context: A fair six-sided die is rolled 4 times. Separately, a pair of fair six-sided dice is rolled 24 times. (This pair of problems is a famous historical question first posed to Blaise Pascal in the 17th century.)
statements: The probability of rolling at least one 6 in 4 rolls of a single die is greater than 50%.
The probability of rolling at least one 6 in 4 rolls equals 1 − (5/6)⁴.
The probability of rolling no 6 at all in the 4 rolls is less than 45%.
The probability of rolling at least one double-six in 24 rolls of a pair of dice is less than 50%.
The probability of rolling at least one double-six in 24 rolls of a pair of dice is greater than the probability of rolling at least one 6 in 4 rolls of a single die.
tactical_explanations:
Statement A — True

$$
P(at least one 6) = 1 − (5/6)⁴
$$

= 51.77%, which is greater than 50%.

The statement is true.

Statement B — True

$$
P(at least one 6 in 4 rolls) = 1 − (5/6)⁴
$$

This is exactly the complement-rule formula applied to 4 independent rolls, each with a 5/6 chance of avoiding a 6.

The statement is true.

Statement C — False

$$
P(no 6 in 4 rolls) = (5/6)⁴
$$

= 48.23%, which is not less than 45%.

The statement is false. A student who applied the complementary count or swapped the inequality direction would mark the statement true.

Statement D — True

$$
P(at least one double-six) = 1 − (35/36)²⁴
$$

= 49.14%, which is less than 50%.

The statement is true.

Statement E — False

$$
Compare 49.14\% (double-six, 24 rolls) to 51.77\% (single 6, 4 rolls)
$$

= 49.14%.

The statement is false. A student who applied the complementary count or swapped the inequality direction would mark the statement true (49.14%).
tasks.solution_overview: Apply the complement rule to each independent-trials scenario.

tasks.title: A Bookshelf Restriction
tasks.context: 5 distinct fiction novels and 3 distinct mystery novels (8 books total, all different) are arranged at random in a row on a shelf.
statements: The total number of possible arrangements is 40,320.
The number of arrangements in which no two mystery novels are adjacent to each other is 14,400.
The probability that no two mystery novels are adjacent is 5/14.
The probability that all three mystery novels are adjacent (sitting together as a block) is greater than the probability that no two mystery novels are adjacent.
The probability that no two mystery novels are adjacent is more than 3 times the probability that all three mystery novels are adjacent.
tactical_explanations:
Statement A — True

$$
Total arrangements = 8!
$$

The statement is true.

Statement B — True

$$
No-two-adjacent arrangements = 5!·{}_{6}P_{3} = 120·120 = 14,400
$$

Arranging the 5 fiction novels (5! ways) and placing the 3 mystery novels into 3 of the 6 available gaps in order (_6P_3 = 120 ways) gives 5!·_6P_3 = 120·120 = 14,400.

The statement is true.

Statement C — True

$$
P(no two mystery novels adjacent) = 14,400/40,320 = 5/14
$$

14,400/40,320 simplifies exactly to 5/14, matching the probability from Step 1.

The statement is true.

Statement D — False

$$
Compare 3/28
$$

$$
= 3/28
$$

= 35.71%.

P(no two adjacent) = 5/14

The statement is false. A student who applied the complementary count or swapped the inequality direction would mark the statement true.

Statement E — True

$$
Compare (5/14)/(3/28) = 10/3
$$

$$
= 140/42
$$

= 3.33.

The statement is true.
tasks.solution_overview: Apply the gap method: arrange the 5 fiction novels first, then place the 3 mystery novels into the gaps between and around them.

tasks.title: Find the Missing Value (12)
tasks.context: A security code is formed by arranging 3 different digits, in order, chosen from a set of n available digits (no digit repeats within a code). The total number of possible 3-digit codes is 336.
statements: The unknown value n equals 8.
If codes were instead 4 digits long (still no repeats, still order matters, same n), the number of possible codes would be 1,680.
The number of ways to choose (unordered) 3 digits from the n available digits is 56.
If the number of possible 3-digit codes had been 720 instead of 336, n would equal 10.
The number of ways to arrange all n digits in a row (n!) is greater than 50,000.
tactical_explanations:
Statement A — True

$$
Solve {}_{n}P_{3} = 336 for n
$$

Solving _nP_3 = 336 gives n(n−1)(n−2) = 336, and n = 8 satisfies this (8·7·6 = 336), as found in Step 1.

The statement is true.

Statement B — True

$$
{}_{8}P_{4} = 8·7·6·5 = 1,680
$$

With n = 8, _8P_4 = 8·7·6·5 = 1,680, confirming the statement.

The statement is true.

Statement C — True

$$
\binom{8}{3} = 8·7·6/3! = 56
$$

With n = 8, C83 = 8!/(3!·5!) = 56, confirming the statement.

The statement is true.

Statement D — True

$$
Solve n(n−1)(n−2) = 720 for n
$$

Re-solving n(n−1)(n−2) = 720 gives n = 10, since 10·9·8 = 720, confirming the statement.

The statement is true.

Statement E — False

$$
8! = 40,320
$$

The statement is false. 8! = 40,320, — it is somewhat less worth double-checking rather than assuming factorials are always "large."
tasks.solution_overview: Solve for n using the permutation count, since the 3-digit code has order-matters and no-repeats.

tasks.title: Choosing a Committee
tasks.context: A club has 8 men and 5 women (13 members total). A committee of 5 members is selected at random from the 13.
statements: The total number of possible 5-person committees is 1,287.
The probability that the committee has exactly 3 men and 2 women is greater than 43.5%.
The probability that the committee has at least 4 women is less than 3.2%.
It is impossible for the committee to contain no men at all, since only 5 women are available.
The probability that the committee includes at least 1 woman is more than 30 times the probability that it includes at least 4 women.
tactical_explanations:
Statement A — True

$$
Total committees = \binom{13}{5}
$$

$$
= 1,287
$$

= 1,287.

The statement is true.

Statement B — True

$$
P(3M, 2W) = \binom{8}{3}\cdot \binom{5}{2}/\binom{13}{5} = 560/1,287
$$

$$
= 560/1,287
$$

= 43.5120%.

The statement is true.

Statement C — True

$$
P(≥4 women) = [\binom{8}{1}\cdot \binom{5}{4} + \binom{5}{5}]/\binom{13}{5} = 41/1,287
$$

$$
= 41/1,287
$$

= 3.1857%.

The statement is true.

Statement D — False

$$
Ways with 0 men = \binom{8}{0}\cdot \binom{5}{5} = 1
$$

The statement is false. A student who applied the complementary count or swapped the inequality direction would mark the statement true.

Statement E — True

tasks.title: Mismatched Gifts (Derangements)
tasks.context: 6 friends each bring one wrapped gift to a party. The gifts are shuffled and redistributed uniformly at random, one to each friend - every one of the 6! possible assignments is equally likely.
statements: The total number of ways to redistribute the 6 gifts is 720.
The probability that no friend receives their own gift is greater than 36.8%.
The probability that exactly one friend receives their own gift is greater than the probability that no friend receives their own gift.
The probability that exactly two friends receive their own gifts is exactly 3/16.
The probability that every friend receives their own original gift (the identity assignment) is greater than 1 in 500.
tactical_explanations:
Statement A — True

$$
Total assignments = 6!
$$

The statement is true.

Statement B — True

$$
P(no matches) = D₆/6! = 265/720
$$

$$
= 265/720
$$

= 36.8056%.

The statement is true.

Statement C — False

$$
Compare \binom{6}{1}·D₅/6! = 264/720 to D₆/6! = 265/720
$$

$$
= 264/720
$$

= 36.6667%.

The statement is false. A student who applied the complementary count or swapped the inequality direction would mark the statement true.
